title: slab allocator and cbatch interplay - scratchpad
content:
Objective:
Quick scratchpad to capture commands, signals, and hypotheses about a throughput regression that looks tied to the slab allocator interacting badly with the continuous batcher (cbatch). Trying to keep a runnable checklist for reproductions and next steps.

Symptoms (observed):
- Production latency SLOs hit for medium tail on small models (redwood-ggml-7B-repl) since 2024-11-03 deploy.
- Median latency unchanged but p95/p99 increased.
- Throughput on affected node pool fell ~38% during peak traffic windows: ~15k tokens/s -> ~9.3k tokens/s (per-node aggregates).
- Continuous-batcher windows occasionally spike from configured 20ms to ~120ms, leading to larger-than-expected microbatches and queuing.
- Memory allocator stats show more heap arenas in use and larger fragmentation (see jemalloc snapshot below).

Timeline / quick events:
- 2024-11-03 02:14 UTC: Release 2024.11.3 (runtime change: switch default allocator to 'slab-allocator-v2' under flag --use-slab).
- 2024-11-04 09:45 UTC: First throughput alert during regional surge.
- 2024-11-05 01:30 UTC: Canary nodes show oscillation, dev nodes fine.
- 2024-11-05 14:00 UTC: Reverted slab flag on 2 canaries (partial mitigation) -> throughput recovered to ~85% but not fully to pre-release baseline.

Commands / traces I've run (copyable):
- kubectl exec -n runtime -it pod/<pod> -- sh -c \"RUST_LOG=debug /opt/redwood/bin/runtime serve --config /etc/runtime/conf.yaml 2>&1 | tee /tmp/runtime.log\"
- kubectl logs -n runtime <pod> -c runtime --tail=500 | sed -n '1,200p'
- curl -s -X POST https://canary-host/api/v1/generate -d @sample-payload.json -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -o /tmp/curl.out -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n'
- pprof-like stack sample: perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -- sleep 20; perf report --stdio > /tmp/perf.txt
- dump jemalloc stats via admin socket: echo 'malloc_stats_print' | socat - /var/run/runtime-admin.sock > /tmp/malloc_stats.txt
- grpc trace for batch windows: ./bin/batcher-inspect --host <pod> --window-history 200 --format json > /tmp/window_history.json

Relevant log snippets (redacted):
- \"cbatch: window extended, requested=20ms, actual=118ms, queued=42, cause=alloc-latency\"
- \"allocator slab: free slab search 43us, fallback to global arena -> 7.9ms allocation\"
- \"serve::executor: worker stalled for 9ms waiting allocation (size=18432)\"
- \"jemalloc: arenas_active=12, fragmentation_ratio=1.38, small_prof_allocs=9240\"

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Slab allocator path has regression when many small allocations are interleaved with cbatch prefill/prefix-kv operations. The slab search becomes O(N) under certain arena states causing jitter that increases the observed batch window.
2) Continuous batcher is sensitive to allocation tail latency: if a single allocation blocks a worker thread for >max_wait_ms, cbatch extends window to accumulate more requests, increasing queueing and compounding memory pressure. This creates a positive feedback loop.
3) Thread locality mismatch: cbatch worker threads are migrated or pinned incorrectly causing frequent cross-arena allocations (cold arenas) which are expensive.
4) Background GC-like compaction (not GC, but runtime maintenance) runs concurrently and races with allocator, spike correlation seen at 5–10 minute intervals.

Quick experiments/results so far:
- Reverted to old allocator on 2 canaries: p95 improved by ~22% and throughput up ~12% (not full recovery). Suggests allocator is major factor but maybe config/stateful.
- Forcing thread affinity (taskset) on a single test pod reduced arena-crossing events in jemalloc trace but only helped tail on synthetic microbenchmarks, not on production traffic shape.
- Disabled cbatch prefill (experiment flag) on one instance: saw less allocation churn but higher token-per-request latency (expected). Peak throughput recovered modestly.
- Took jemalloc dump: contiguous free extent count decreased and fragmentation spike matched window extensions.

Repro recipe (local-ish):
1) Start runtime with --use-slab and cbatch configured: target_batch_ms=20, max_batch_ms=120, target_tokens=512, prefill=true.
2) Replay real traffic trace (high conc concurrency, low-latency tails): ./tools/replay_traffic --trace traces/2024-11-03-peak.json --rps 800
3) Collect malloc_stats_print every 10s and cbatch window history.
4) Watch for: allocation hiccups >2ms correlating with window extensions.

Short-term mitigations to try (low-risk):
- Rollback --use-slab globally until fix applied (costly but straightforward).
- Tune cbatch to have tighter max_backoff or reduce reliance on allocation timing: set max_batch_ms=60 as emergency config.
- Increase per-thread cache sizes in slab allocator (if config exists) to reduce cross-arena searches.

Longer-term debugging ideas (next week):
- Add instrumentation in slab allocator to emit histograms for search time, fallback counts, and arena hops. Gate behind debug flag.
- Reproduce with deterministic unit test: spawn N threads with cbatch-like allocation pattern, measure allocation time distribution.
- Profile with jemalloc profiling at high frequency and symbolicated flamegraphs.
- Consider switching slab policy to prefer per-thread caches for small objects used by cbatch and KV prefill.

Notes / random observations:
- The 'allocation took 7.9ms' events often coincide with an entry in /proc/interrupts bump (maybe unrelated).
- Not seeing OOM or cgroup pressure; RSS stable but virtual mapping churn high.
- Some older nodes (kernel 5.15) show less severe symptoms than newer ones (5.19) — possible kernel allocator interactions.

Next actions (concrete):
- [Avery] Finish jemalloc trace capture for two canaries (due 2024-11-06).
- [Ravi] Add a debug flag in slab allocator to emit fallback counts and microsecond hist (due 2024-11-08).
- [Maya] Run large-scale replay with that flag on staging and collect cbatch window traces (due 2024-11-09).
- If staging reproduces: plan rollback or configuration change in 2024-11-10 maintenance window.

Anything to add? Scratch notes here so I don't lose command history.
